title: Bhai Sangat Singh
hook: tradition says a Sikh who looked like the Guru wore his plume at Chamkaur so the Guru could slip away

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rest of the five: Dharam Singh who lived on, and three who fell at Chamkaur. Your line was the five, remembered. Whose name from your back row did you say? Today, we stay at Chamkaur one more night. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

Night at Chamkaur. The mud-walled house is ringed by an army that will attack again at first light. Inside, only a handful of Sikhs are left. They have already told the Guru he must go, so the community will not lose him. The Guru has agreed. But an army watches a house like this. If the Guru's tall plume disappears from the wall, they'll know. Someone has to stay behind and be seen. Someone who, in the dark and at a distance, could pass for him. Today: Bhai Sangat Singh.
screen: `NIGHT, AND AN ARMY OUTSIDE.` → `THE GURU MUST GO.` → `SOMEONE MUST BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Bhai Sangat Singh looked like Guru Gobind Singh, close enough in look and build that, from below, in poor light, he could be taken for him. So before the Guru left, he gave Sangat Singh his own plume, the kalgi, a jeweled ornament worn on the turban, along with his garments. Sangat Singh put them on and took the Guru's place in the house, where the enemy could see him. Then, in the dark, the Guru slipped out with a few companions. When morning came, the army attacked the house again, believing the Guru was inside. Sangat Singh and the Sikhs with him fought until they fell. Tradition says the enemy at first thought they had killed the Guru himself. Look at what he did, and what it wasn't. It wasn't a trick for its own sake. It was a gift of time. Every hour the soldiers spent watching the plume on the wall was an hour the Guru was further away. Sangat Singh wasn't taking the Guru's honor. He was taking the Guru's danger. Some tellings give part of this story to another Sikh, Bhai Sant Singh, and some speak of the two together. The details shift between tellings, but the shape stays the same: a Sikh who put on what marked the Guru, and stood where the Guru would have stood, so the Guru could live. Sikhs call his name with love. He is remembered not for looking like the Guru, but for what he did with that likeness.
screen: `HE LOOKED LIKE THE GURU.` · `THE KALGI ON HIS TURBAN.` · `A GIFT OF TIME.` · `TAKING THE DANGER, NOT THE HONOR.` · then, large: `HE TOOK HIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cover for someone kindly. This isn't about lying for anyone. It's about stepping into a hard spot so someone else can get through. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone near you who's carrying too much right now. A coworker who's behind. A parent who hasn't had a night off. A friend facing something they dread. Ask quietly: what could I take on, so they could slip away for a while? A shift. A dinner. A phone call they keep putting off. Just find the one thing. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Sangat Singh. The Sikh who, tradition says, wore the Guru's plume at Chamkaur and stood in his place, so the Guru could get away. Today's word.
Your line: he took his place. Today, take one weight off someone else, a task, a shift, a hard call, so they can step away for a while. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Sangat Singh in remembrances of Chamkaur, especially in December when the martyrdoms of that season are recalled, and the gurdwara at Chamkaur keeps the memory of those who fell there.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kalgi, the plume worn on the turban; Guru Gobind Singh is sometimes called the one with the plume.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man who happened to look like the Guru.
what it means: a Sikh who, tradition says, put on the Guru's plume and stood in his place so the Guru could escape.
what a scholar hears: the tellings vary on names and details, Sangat Singh, Sant Singh, or both, but agree on the core: the Guru's marker worn by a Sikh to draw the danger.

notes: Resemblance to the Guru, the gift of the kalgi and garments, and the enemy's belief that they had killed the Guru: all given as 'tradition says'; confirm.
Sant Singh / Sangat Singh: some accounts make Sant Singh the one who wore the plume and Sangat Singh his companion. The script names both without deciding; a Keeper should decide.
The Guru's companions on leaving (often named as Daya Singh, Dharam Singh and Man Singh) given only as 'a few companions'.
'Close enough in age and build' is a softened version of the tradition that they were alike; confirm.
Original note: 'the one with the plume' alludes to the epithet Kalgidhar; confirm.
